intuition: If the total is odd, two equal sums are impossible. Otherwise, try to reach half the total with some of the numbers. Save which sums are possible as you process each number. The numbers left out will automatically have the other half if the target is reached.

This is a 0/1 selection problem, not a contiguous-window problem. reachable[s] records whether processed elements can make sum s. Sum zero begins reachable because the empty subset is always available. When a value arrives, each subtotal can remain reachable without it or become reachable by extending a previously reachable subtotal-value.

The one-dimensional table must be updated backward. A forward scan would read entries already created by the current value and effectively allow that value to be selected several times. Descending order reads only the state from before including this value. The resulting table retains all possible subset sums up to the target while discarding irrelevant larger sums.
Duplicate values are still separate input elements, so each copy gets its own update pass.

Strictly positive inputs let us discard sums above target: adding another value can never bring them back down. Negative values would invalidate that truncation; zeros are outside this problem's domain, though a 0/1 subset DP can handle them with care.
Once target is reachable, later values can be excluded from the chosen subset, so the reference returns early without losing a valid partition.

steps: For nums=[1,5,11,5], total=22 and target=11. Initialize only reachable[0] to true.
Processing 1 adds sum 1, leaving reachable sums {0,1}.
Processing the first 5 adds sums 5 and 6, so the set is {0,1,5,6}.
Processing 11 makes target 11 reachable directly from sum zero. Backward updates do not reuse the same 11.
The target is now reachable, so return true immediately without processing the final 5. The chosen subset [11] leaves complementary values [1,5,5], which also sum to 11.

codeNotes.note: Parity rules out equal integer sums before allocating or updating the dynamic-programming table.
Descending sums ensure each input occurrence contributes at most once, maintaining 0/1 rather than unlimited selection.
The two possibilities correspond to excluding the current value or including it after an already constructible smaller sum.

keyDecision: Update possible sums from high to low so the current input occurrence is used at most once.

figures.title: Why sum updates go backward
figures.caption: The example starts by processing value 1 with target 11. Each occurrence may be chosen only once.

panels.title: Before: only zero is reachable
panels.note: The empty subset makes sum 0. No positive sum is reachable yet.

panels.title: Check: scan from 11 down to 1
panels.note: When checking sum 2, sum 1 is still false. Only afterward does sum 1 become true from sum 0.

panels.title: After: one new sum
panels.note: Reachable sums are {0, 1}. A forward scan would wrongly reuse this same 1 to make 2, 3, and more.

concept.question: How does reaching half the total settle the whole partition?
intuition: Enumerating both subsets duplicates the same decision: once one subset is chosen, the other consists of everything left. Equal totals require one subset to reach half the overall total.

If the total is even, track reachable subset sums through its half. Each value can extend sums reachable before that value was used. Update from larger sums downward so one occurrence cannot extend itself repeatedly.
concept.observation: Each input occurrence may be used at most once; new sums must extend older reachability.
approach: Begin with only sum zero reachable.
For each value, mark newly reachable sums downward and check the half-total target.
concept.correctness: Before each value, the marked totals are exactly the sums of subsets of earlier occurrences. Keeping old marks represents exclusion; extending them by this value represents inclusion. Downward traversal keeps every predecessor from the earlier stage, so no occurrence is reused. Reaching half the total is equivalent to an equal partition.

complexity.explanation: For every value, scan totals up to half the sum. Time is proportional to item count times that target; storage is one target-sized reachability table.

pitfalls: Each input occurrence may be used at most once; new sums must extend older reachability.
Do not update upward, which would allow unlimited copies.

scenes.title: Aim at half the total
scenes.narration: For [1,5,11,5], total 22 gives target 11. Zero is initially reachable using no values.
scenes.decision: A subset reaching 11 leaves another subset totaling exactly 11.

scenes.title: Build distinct reachable sums
scenes.narration: After 1, reachable sums are 0 and 1. After the first 5, sums 5 and 6 are added.
scenes.decision: Downward updates prevent using this same 5 twice.

scenes.title: Eleven reaches the target
scenes.narration: The value 11 extends zero directly to the target. The complementary values 1,5,5 also total 11. Return yes.
scenes.decision: Once the target is reachable, the remaining values need no further decisions.
